papers.what_it_is: An empirical comparison of three hybrid quantum neural networks (QuanNN, QCNN, QTL) on a four-class MNIST subset, followed by a simulated noise-robustness study of QuanNN and QCNN under five noise channels.

existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
The paper states the limit itself in Section 2.2 (QCNN description), p.4.

existing.note: The comparison in the noise analysis is between QuanNN and QCNN only: Quantum Transfer Learning was dropped after the noise-free stage. The paper's own results show cases where QuanNN is not the more robust one (see the QCNN amplitude damping, phase damping and phase flip results versus the QuanNN amplitude damping and bit flip results). The Conclusion drops the abstract's 'in most scenarios'.
existing.value: The authors report that, in most scenarios, the Quanvolutional Neural Network shows greater robustness across the quantum noise channels tested than the other model compared in the noise analysis, the QCNN (Quantum Transfer Learning was excluded from that analysis after the noise-free comparison), and that it consistently outperforms the other models; the Conclusion states the outperformance without the words 'in most scenarios'.

papers.title_in_file: Towards Quantum Graph Neural Networks: An Ego-Graph Learning Approach
papers.version_note: arXiv:2201.05158v3 (19 Jan 2024), the IEEE-style preprint. The file name says 2022 and Decompositional-Quantum-Graph-Neural-Network (an earlier title); the text is the v3 text. Page numbers in anchors are PDF pages (form-feed chunks); they differ by up to two from the page numbers in the brief (the brief puts the OriginQ sentence on p.8; it is on PDF p.10). The reference list has duplicated or mis-numbered entries (for example [9] repeats the R-GCN paper where the text means Cong et al.), and the appendix labels Theorem 1 as 'Theorem 4'.
papers.what_it_is: A proposal of a hybrid quantum-classical graph neural network (egoQGNN) that processes ego-graphs on a small quantum circuit, with a trainable mapping of node features to qubit states, a graph-isomorphism argument, and simulator experiments on six graph-classification benchmarks.

existing.value: The authors list achieving exponential speed-up with quantum techniques as a long-term goal.
quotes: a long-term goal, quantum techniques need to be utilized to achieve exponential speed-up.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors state it as future work; the paper does not test or show a speed-up.
existing.reader_inference: The sentence is an open problem the authors name. It implies the present egoQGNN, run on a classical simulator, is not claimed to give a speed-up.

existing.note: The abstract says 'outperforms ... only 1.68% parameters'. The contributions list (p.1-2) narrows it twice: the 1.68% is relative to one model, the GNN with the fewest parameters (DGCNN), and the performance is 'similar', not better. Section 5.3.1 also says egoQGNN does not win on every benchmark.
existing.value: The authors report that egoQGNN achieves a similar performance with only 1.68% of the parameters of DGCNN, the GNN model with the least parameters; the abstract words the same figure as outperforming competitive state-of-the-art models with only 1.68% parameters compared to those models.
quotes: the egoQGNN achieves a similar performance but with only 1.68% of the parameters when compared with the GNN model with the least parameters, DGCNN [31].
Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms competitive state-of-the-art models with only 1.68% parameters compared to those models.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, run on a simulator.
existing.reader_inference: Table 5 (PDF p.11) lists 2,560 parameters for DGCNN and 43 for egoQGNN; 43 / 2560 is 1.68%, so the percentage is against DGCNN only, and against the other deep models it is smaller. The abstract's 'outperforms' is stronger than the contribution list's 'similar performance'.

existing.note: Better quotes added: the paper also says why, and that every reported experiment is a simulation. The sentence is on PDF p.10, not p.8.
existing.value: The authors state that the method is implemented using the OriginQ simulator on a classical computer.
quotes: The proposed method is implemented using the OriginQ [61] simulator on a classical computer.
For this reason, all of the reported experiments are performed using a simulator running on a classical computer.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section 5.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of the lack of physical qubits and of an effective means to map real-world data from Euclidean space to Hilbert space, most existing quantum machine learning methods focus on quantum analogies or process simulations rather than concrete architectures based on qubits.
quotes: most of these methods focus on quantum analogies or process simulations rather than devising concrete architectures based on qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' characterization of other work; no survey evidence is given for the word 'most'.

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 1: the tensor product is injective for non-zero vectors with the same dimension, and so maps them to different representations unless they are linearly dependent vectors. The proof is in the Appendix.
assertions.anchor: Lemma 1, Section 4.1, p.5; proof in Appendix p.11-12
quotes: Lemma 1. The tensor product is injective, for non-zero vectors with the same dimension.
the tensor product maps them to different representations unless they are linearly dependent vectors.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted, but it is worded so that it is not injective in the usual sense (it excludes linearly dependent vectors) and the appendix proof is a sketch for real vectors; a grader should not take this as a clean proved result.
assertions.reader_inference: As written, A tensor B equals (cA) tensor (B/c) for any non-zero scalar c, so the map is not injective on pairs of vectors; the lemma's own exception clause covers this. The text then says 'all quantum states are linearly independent', which is false for states in the same space (a state and a phase multiple of it are dependent).

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 2: if two quantum states A and B are linearly dependent, and B = k times A, then k = plus or minus 1. The appendix proof takes k to be a real number and uses the unit norm of both states.
assertions.anchor: Lemma 2, Section 4.1, p.5; proof in Appendix p.12
quotes: Lemma 2. If two quantum states A and B are linearly dependent, and B = k · A, then k = ±1.
B = k · A, k ∈ R.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted and the appendix proof (k squared times 1 equals 1) is complete for real k.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof assumes k is real. For complex k the same normalization only gives modulus 1 (a global phase), so the lemma as stated in the main text omits a condition that the appendix adds.

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 3: for different nodes v and mu, the outputs of its Eq. 10, the states of v and mu, are not equal. The appendix proof splits into nodes with different numbers of neighbors (different dimensions) and nodes with the same number of neighbors (using the two earlier lemmas).
assertions.anchor: Lemma 3, Section 4.1, p.5; proof in Appendix p.12
quotes: Lemma 3. For different nodes v and µ, the outputs of Eq. 10: |φv⟩ and |φµ⟩, meet |φv⟩ ≠ |φµ⟩.
If v and µ have different numbers of neighbors, the dimensions of |φv⟩ and |φµ⟩t−1 are different.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted, but the proof's same-neighbor-count case concludes inequality from Lemmas 1 and 2 without using the node features or neighborhoods, so the argument is incomplete.
assertions.reader_inference: Two different nodes with identical features and identical neighbor multisets would give identical states under any deterministic circuit, so 'different nodes' must mean nodes with different features or neighborhoods; the lemma as stated does not say this, though the text before it does.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 1: the egoQGNN maps two non-isomorphic graphs G1 and G2, as decided via a GNN by its Eq. 10, to different embeddings. The appendix proof (labelled with a different theorem number there) uses the earlier lemmas to get unequal node states and then unequal summed entropies.
assertions.anchor: Theorem 1, Section 4.1, p.5; proof in Appendix p.12
quotes: Theorem 1. The egoQGNN maps two non-isomorphic graphs G1 and G2 as decided via a GNN by Eq. 10 to different embeddings.
So, egoQGNN can distinguish graphs that are decided as non-isomorphic by GNNs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted, but the proof moves from unequal node states to unequal graph sums with 'Moreover' and no argument, and the graph representation is a sum of entropies of pure states (see the definition assertion).
assertions.reader_inference: A sum of per-node scalar entropies can coincide for different multisets of node states, so unequal node states do not imply unequal sums. The paper does not show the entropies are injective. Also, the von Neumann entropy of a pure state is zero, so as written (rho = |phi><phi|) every graph would get the same representation; the paper does not say how mixed states arise.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 2: for the same inputs, its Eq. 16 (the split-neighbor-set computation) is equivalent to its Eq. 10. The text says the proof is in the Appendix.
quotes: Theorem 2. For the same inputs, Eq. 16 is equivalent to Eq. 10.
We provide proof of this theorem in the Appendix.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted, but the text layer's appendix holds proofs of Lemma 1, Lemma 2, Lemma 3 and the isomorphism theorem and no proof of Theorem 2.
assertions.reader_inference: The appendix in this version has no section headed for Theorem 2, so the claimed proof is missing from the text read. The result is plausible because splitting a tensor product of unitary images into groups and recombining it is associative, but the paper does not show it.

assertions.value: The authors state that egoQGNN has only n times max(log2 d, log2 h) variational parameters if n quantum gates are applied to each qubit, against d times h parameters for a classical GNN layer mapping d dimensions to h dimensions, because a unitary matrix has one variational parameter.
quotes: Such a layer has d × h parameters that need to be trained.
The egoQGNN has only n · max(log2 d, log2 h) variational parameters for training if n quantum gates are applied to each qubit.
This is because a unitary matrix has only one variational parameter (the rotation of the quantum states).
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by the authors, not a proved or measured result.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 4.2 gives three rotation gates per qubit, each with its own parameter (RX, RY, RZ), which conflicts with 'one variational parameter' per unitary; Table 5 reports 43 parameters, not a multiple of three.

assertions.value: The authors state that with the ego-graph decomposition the number of qubits needed to compute a graph's representation falls from N to D, where N is the number of nodes and D is the maximum degree of the graph, and that when fewer qubits n than D are available the neighbor set can be split into disjoint subsets of size at most n.
quotes: the number of qubits required to compute its representation is accordingly reduced from N to D by introducing the above ego-graph decomposition, where D is the maximum degree of the graph.
If the number of available qubits n < D, we can divide the neighbour sets
assertions.certainty_reason: A design claim of the method; no experiment on hardware tests it.
assertions.reader_inference: The reduction assumes the representation of one node needs qubits only for that node's neighbors; the qubit count for the von Neumann entropy step or for the error-correction ancillas is not added in.

assertions.value: The paper defines an ego-graph as a central node and all of its connected neighbors, and the decomposition strategy divides a graph with N nodes into N ego-graphs (one per node) on a classical computer, processes them sequentially on the quantum circuit, and merges the representations on the classical computer.
quotes: An ego-graph consists of a central node and all of its connected neighbors.
The number of ego-graph is equal to the number of nodes.
the quantum circuits process each ego-graph sequentially and return their representations to the classical computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition and procedure in Sections 1 and 4.4.

assertions.value: The paper defines the graph representation as the von Neumann entropy of each node's quantum state summed over all nodes of the graph, used to characterize the graph for classification.
quotes: To classify graphs, their von Neumann entropy is summed over the quantum states of all nodes and used as a characterization of the graph.
hG = Σv∈GS(ρv), ρv = |φv⟩⟨φv|
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition (Eq. 17-18).
assertions.reader_inference: With rho_v = |phi_v><phi_v| the state is pure and its von Neumann entropy is 0, so as defined the representation is 0 for every graph. The paper does not explain how it avoids this (for example by tracing out qubits).

assertions.value: The authors state that classification uses two reference quantum states for the two classes, corresponding to the upper and lower Bloch hemispheres, and that this approach is essentially the same as QSVM; a graph gets the label of the class whose reference entropy is nearer its representation.
quotes: Our approach is essentially the same as QSVM.
We use two quantum states corresponding to two classes, and these correspond to the upper and lower Bloch hemispheres.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its decision rule.
assertions.reader_inference: The rule compares scalar entropies, while QSVM measures a Pauli-Z component; 'essentially the same' is the authors' wording and is looser than the equations.

assertions.value: The paper defines a trainable mapping from data to quantum states whose loss is the difference between normalized Euclidean distances between samples and normalized inverse-cosine distances between the corresponding quantum states on the Bloch sphere, and states the aim is to maintain distance relations and reduce information loss.
quotes: we present a mapping method in which the loss is related to the difference in the distance relations between the Euclidean space and the Bloch sphere.
We utilize the inverse cosine of the inner product of the quantum states for distance measure.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its mapping loss (Section 4.3).
assertions.reader_inference: Algorithm 2 (p.7) computes the data distance as the inner product x_i . x_j rather than a Euclidean distance, which differs from the prose.

assertions.value: The authors state that the egoQGNN circuit applies a three-bit error correction code, with copy and recovery modules around the Ulayer, to protect the target node's state from noise.
quotes: Considering the likely effects of noise interference on quantum devices, we apply the three-bit error correction
Following the three-bit error correction code proposed by [45]
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own circuit design.
assertions.reader_inference: All reported experiments are noiseless simulator runs (see the simulation-only assertion), so the paper reports no test of the error-correction modules.

assertions.value: The authors state that existing quantum coding platforms are unable to provide the fast and effective interaction between a classical computer and a quantum computer that the framework needs, and for this reason all reported experiments run on a simulator on a classical computer.
quotes: As yet existing quantum coding platforms [59], [60] are unable to provide the fast and effective interaction between a classical computer and a quantum computer required by the proposed framework.
all of the reported experiments are performed using a simulator running on a classical computer.

papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that introduces a teacher-student scheme to compare the expressive power of a quantum perceptron (QP) architecture, deeper QNNs built from QPs, and the data re-uploading (RU) architecture on two-qubit, two-input circuits.

existing.value: The authors state that the aim of the work is to introduce a teacher-student scheme that could systematically compare any QNN architectures and evaluate their relative expressive power.
quotes: The aim of this work is to introduce a teacher-student scheme that could systematically compare any QNN architectures and evaluate their relative expressive power.
existing.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's own aim and setup.

existing.value: The authors state that the deep structures built from quantum perceptrons only increase the expressivity of a model if the data are uploaded several times.
quotes: we showed that the deep structures that can be built with QPs only increase the expressivity of a model if the data are uploaded several times.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result of simulations from one study on one two-input, two-qubit data encoding; no proof is given.
existing.reader_inference: The evidence is the comparison of the single-perceptron circuit, the deep QP circuit and the two-perceptron network in the paper's Fig. 4 and Fig. 5, with loss curves and prediction maps for one example each. The paper reports no repeat statistics for those three circuits.

existing.note: The paper makes this statement inside Section 5.1, titled Toy model, which it introduces as an illustrative example, and it says 'Even for this toy example' about the four metrics. The scope is the toy model: the RU and QP circuits of Fig. 1, two-dimensional inputs, and 10 random initializations of the teacher. The anchor is also corrected: the passage is Section 5.1 on p.5 (printed page footer), not Section 5 p.6. The QP student is not at zero error on the RU teacher: its average relative entropy is 0.247 against 0.001 for the RU student.
existing.value: The authors report, for their toy model (an illustrative teacher-student example with 10 random initializations of the teacher), that the RU architecture can generate and learn more complex output distributions than the QP: it can learn all the data sets generated by the QP with almost zero loss and relative entropy, while the QP is not able to learn the data sets provided by the RU.

We generated 10 different data sets by randomly initializing the teacher
